units.title: Number – Counting, Place Value and Numbers up to 1000

sessions.title: Counting and Writing Numbers up to 200
indicators: Count forward and backward from 0 to 200
Read and write numerals up to 200
Write number words up to 200
Identify the place value of digits in numbers up to 200 (hundreds, tens, ones)
Work in pairs to build numbers with base ten blocks (collaboration)
Use digital number charts and place value apps (digital literacy)
Apply counting skills in real-life situations like counting money or items (personal development)
sessions.content:
Numbers Everywhere – Up to 200

We can count far beyond 100. In Grade 2, we learn numbers up to 200 and understand the value of each digit.

1. Counting Forward and Backward

Count aloud: 101, 102, 103... up to 200. Then try counting backward from 200: 200, 199, 198...
Skip counting by 2s, 5s and 10s up to 200 is also important.

Examples: 134 is one hundred and thirty-four. 189 is one hundred and eighty-nine. The digit 1 in 150 means one hundred, 5 means fifty (five tens), 0 means zero ones.

2. Place Value – Hundreds, Tens, Ones

We use a place value chart:

HundredsTensOnes
152

This means 152 = 1 hundred + 5 tens + 2 ones = 100 + 50 + 2.

Activity 1 – Build it with blocks
In pairs, use base ten blocks (hundred flats, ten rods, unit cubes). One partner says a number between 100 and 200, the other builds it and writes the numeral. Swap roles. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Number word match
Match cards with numerals (e.g., 173) to cards with words (one hundred and seventy-three). Play memory. (collaboration).

Digital corner: Use an interactive hundred chart that goes up to 200. Click a number to hear it read aloud and see its place value breakdown. (digital literacy).

Exercise 1.1

  1. Write the numeral for one hundred and forty-seven.
  2. What number is 1 hundred + 3 tens + 9 ones?
  3. Count backward from 200 to 190. Write the numbers.
  4. In 168, what is the value of the digit 6?

sessions.title: Numbers up to 500 – Place Value and Ordering
indicators: Read and write numerals up to 500
Decompose numbers into hundreds, tens and ones
Compare numbers using greater than, less than and equal to
Order a set of numbers from smallest to largest
Work in groups to order number cards (collaboration)
Use digital place value games to reinforce understanding (digital literacy)
Recognise number patterns in the environment (personal development)
sessions.content:
Bigger Numbers – Up to 500

We extend our counting to 500. The pattern is the same: hundreds, tens and ones.

1. Reading and Writing

Examples: 256 = two hundred and fifty-six. 409 = four hundred and nine (no tens). 370 = three hundred and seventy (no ones).

2. Comparing Numbers

Use symbols: greater than ( > ), less than ( < ), equal to ( = ). Compare the hundreds first, then tens, then ones.
Example: 342 > 289 because 3 hundreds > 2 hundreds. 165 < 170 because tens (6 tens < 7 tens).

Activity 1 – Number line order
Draw a number line from 300 to 400. Mark given numbers on it. Discuss which is larger or smaller. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Greater than gator
Use a paper cut-out of a crocodile's mouth that always wants to eat the bigger number. Pupils place the gator correctly between two number cards. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a virtual place value chart where pupils can drag digits and see the number instantly. (digital literacy).

Exercise 1.2

  1. Write 3 hundreds + 4 tens + 7 ones as a numeral.
  2. Which is larger: 398 or 402? Explain why.
  3. Order from smallest to largest: 456, 298, 512, 345.
  4. Write the number that is 10 more than 390.

sessions.title: Numbers up to 1000 – Counting, Place Value and Patterns
indicators: Count forward and backward up to 1000
Read and write numerals up to 1000
Identify the place value of digits in 3-digit numbers
Recognise patterns when counting by 10s and 100s
Work with a partner to sequence numbers to 1000 (collaboration)
Use digital interactive 1000-charts (digital literacy)
Build confidence in handling larger numbers (personal development)
sessions.content:
To a Thousand and Beyond

1000 is ten hundreds. We can count all the way there and understand the value of each digit.

1. Place Value up to 1000

HundredsTensOnes
999

999 = 9 hundreds + 9 tens + 9 ones. Add 1 more: 10 hundreds = 1000.

Examples: 605 = six hundred and five. 730 = seven hundred and thirty. 1000 = one thousand.

Activity 1 – Thousand chain
In groups, use linking chains or paper clips to make a chain of 1000 links, grouping by 10s, 100s. Count together. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – 1000 chart puzzle
Give each group a section of a 1000-chart. They assemble it in order and discuss patterns (all numbers in a column end with the same digit). (collaboration).

Digital corner: Use a digital 1000-chart to colour multiples of 5, 10, 100 and observe patterns. (digital literacy).

Exercise 1.3

  1. Write the numeral for eight hundred and twelve.
  2. Decompose 784 into hundreds, tens and ones.
  3. What number is 10 less than 1000?
  4. Count by 100s from 100 to 1000. Write the numbers.

units.title: Operations – Addition and Subtraction (with and without regrouping)

sessions.title: Addition of 2-Digit Numbers (without regrouping)
indicators: Add two 2-digit numbers without regrouping (sums up to 99)
Use the column method to set out addition
Add tens and ones separately
Solve simple word problems involving addition
Work in pairs to use number lines for addition (collaboration)
Use digital addition games with immediate feedback (digital literacy)
Develop mental math skills for quick addition (personal development)
sessions.content:
Adding Bigger Numbers – No Regrouping

When we add two 2-digit numbers and the ones don't make more than 9, we just add the tens and ones separately.

1. Column Method

Write numbers vertically, lining up tens and ones. Add the ones column, then the tens column.

Example:

 34
+ 25
----
 59

Ones: 4+5=9. Tens: 3+2=5. Answer 59.

Another: 51 + 37 = 88.

Activity 1 – Dice addition
Roll two dice to make a 2-digit number (e.g., first die tens, second die ones). Roll again for a second number. Add them without regrouping. Check with base ten blocks. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Number line jumps
Draw a number line. Start at the larger number and jump forward by tens and ones to add. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use an app like 'SplashLearn' to practise column addition with virtual blocks. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.1

  1. Solve: 42 + 35 = ?, 63 + 24 = ?
  2. Set out in columns: 55 + 33.
  3. Adwoa has 23 oranges and buys 15 more. How many altogether?
  4. Write and solve your own addition word problem.

sessions.title: Addition with Regrouping (Carrying)
indicators: Add two 2-digit numbers with regrouping (sums up to 99)
Understand when to regroup 10 ones into 1 ten
Use base ten blocks and place value charts to model regrouping
Work in pairs to explain regrouping steps (collaboration)
Use digital animations that show regrouping (digital literacy)
Build persistence in solving more complex problems (personal development)
sessions.content:
Carrying Over – Regrouping Ones into Tens

When the ones column adds up to 10 or more, we regroup 10 ones as 1 ten and carry it to the tens column.

1. Step-by-Step Regrouping

Example: 27 + 45.
Ones: 7 + 5 = 12. Write 2 ones, carry 1 ten to the tens column.
Tens: 2 + 4 + 1 (carried) = 7.
Answer: 72.

Another: 58 + 36 = 94.

Activity 1 – Base ten regroup
Use base ten blocks. To add 27 and 45, combine 2 rods + 4 rods, and 7 units + 5 units. Exchange 10 units for 1 rod. Count the total. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Carry the basket
Draw a basket next to the tens column. When you have 10 or more ones, put 10 in the basket (carry it) and leave the rest. (creativity).

Digital corner: Watch an animation where units combine, a bubble pops and becomes a ten rod that slides to the tens column. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.2

  1. Solve using regrouping: 38 + 47, 56 + 29.
  2. Explain step-by-step how to add 45 + 28.
  3. There are 48 boys and 37 girls in a school hall. How many children altogether?
  4. Find the missing digit: 3_ + 45 = 82.

sessions.title: Subtraction of 2-Digit Numbers (without and with regrouping)
indicators: Subtract a 2-digit number from another (without regrouping)
Subtract with regrouping (borrowing) when needed
Use place value understanding to decompose tens
Check subtraction with addition
Work in groups to solve subtraction puzzles (collaboration)
Use digital subtraction drills to build fluency (digital literacy)
Apply subtraction to real-life situations (personal development)
sessions.content:
Taking Away Bigger Numbers

Sometimes we subtract and the top ones digit is smaller than the bottom ones. We need to borrow 1 ten (regroup).

1. Subtraction without Regrouping

Example: 67 - 34. Ones: 7-4=3. Tens: 6-3=3. Answer: 33.

2. Subtraction with Regrouping (Borrowing)

Example: 52 - 28. Ones: 2 is less than 8, so borrow 1 ten from the 5 tens (leaving 4 tens). That ten becomes 10 ones. Now we have 12 ones - 8 ones = 4. Tens: 4 - 2 = 2. Answer: 24.

Activity 1 – Base ten borrowing
Model 52 with 5 rods and 2 units. To subtract 28, we must break a rod into 10 units. Then remove 8 units and 2 rods. Count what is left. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Subtraction bingo
Create bingo cards with answers to subtraction problems. Teacher calls the problem, pupils cover the answer. (collaboration).

Digital corner: Use a digital place value mat that shows a ten rod cracking open into 10 ones when borrowing is needed. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.3

  1. Solve: 75 - 41, 83 - 57.
  2. Check 60 - 35 by adding your answer to 35. Do you get 60?
  3. Yaw had 94 marbles. He lost 38. How many are left?
  4. Explain how you borrowed in 41 - 17.

sessions.title: Word Problems – Mixed Addition and Subtraction
indicators: Read and interpret word problems to decide whether to add or subtract
Use bar models or drawings to represent problems
Write number sentences and solve
Work in pairs to create and solve each other's word problems (collaboration, creativity)
Use digital story-problem apps with read-aloud features (digital literacy)
Develop problem-solving skills for everyday situations (personal development)
sessions.content:
Maths Stories – Using Addition and Subtraction

Word problems help us use our maths in real life. We must read carefully to choose the right operation.

1. Clues for Addition and Subtraction

Addition clues: altogether, in all, total, join, combined, sum.
Subtraction clues: left, take away, give away, lost, fewer, how many more, difference.

Example (addition): Esi has 48 stickers. Kofi gives her 27 more. How many stickers does she have now? 48 + 27 = 75.

Example (subtraction): There were 86 mangoes in a basket. 39 were sold. How many are left? 86 - 39 = 47.

Activity 1 – Problem-solving pairs
Each pupil writes a word problem on a card. Swap with a partner, solve and check. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Draw the problem
Represent a given word problem using a bar model or simple drawing before writing the number sentence. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a story-based math app that reads the problem aloud and provides virtual manipulatives to solve it. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.4

  1. There are 56 pupils in Class A and 38 pupils in Class B. How many pupils altogether?
  2. A shop had 120 eggs. 65 were sold. How many remain?
  3. Write a word problem that uses subtraction and solve it.
  4. Kofi thinks 34 + 28 = 52. Is he correct? Explain.

sessions.title: Multiplication as Repeated Addition and Groups
indicators: Understand multiplication as repeated addition (e.g., 3+3+3 = 3x3)
Use equal groups and arrays to represent multiplication
Write multiplication sentences using the x and = signs
Work in pairs to build equal groups with counters (collaboration)
Use digital array builders to visualise multiplication (digital literacy)
Relate multiplication to everyday situations like grouping (personal development)
sessions.content:
Groups of Things – Multiplication Starts Here

Multiplication is a quick way to add equal groups. Instead of saying 2+2+2+2=8, we can say 4 groups of 2 is 8, or 4 x 2 = 8.

1. Equal Groups

If you have 3 bowls with 4 apples each, that is 3 groups of 4. Total apples: 4+4+4=12. So 3 x 4 = 12.

Activity 1 – Group and count
Use counters. Make 5 groups of 3. Count them all. Write the repeated addition and the multiplication sentence: 3+3+3+3+3 = 15, 5 x 3 = 15. (collaboration).

2. Arrays

An array is a set of objects in rows and columns. 3 rows of 4 is 3 x 4 = 12.

Activity 2 – Array art
Use stickers or stamps to make an array on paper. Write the multiplication sentence underneath. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a digital array builder to drag dots into rows and columns and see the multiplication sentence. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.1

  1. Draw 4 groups of 5 stars. Write the repeated addition and multiplication sentence.
  2. Write as multiplication: 6 + 6 + 6.
  3. Which array shows 2 x 8? Draw it.
  4. There are 3 bags with 7 balls each. How many balls altogether?

sessions.title: Multiplication Tables – 2, 5, 10
indicators: Recite the 2, 5 and 10 times tables from memory
Use skip counting to find multiples
Solve simple multiplication problems using these tables
Work in pairs to drill multiplication facts (collaboration)
Use digital times table games to build speed and accuracy (digital literacy)
Apply knowledge of tables to quick calculations in daily life (personal development)

Activity 1 – Flashcard frenzy
In pairs, use flashcards for the 2, 5 and 10 times tables. See how many you can answer correctly in one minute. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Times table hopscotch
Draw a hopscotch with multiples of 5. Pupils hop and chant the table. (creativity).

Digital corner: Play an online multiplication game like 'Hit the Button' focusing on 2x, 5x, 10x. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.2

  1. Recite the 5 times table to a family member.
  2. 2 x 8 = ?, 5 x 7 = ?, 10 x 9 = ?.
  3. How many fingers on 6 hands? (Hint: 5 fingers per hand).
  4. There are 4 bags with 10 oranges each. How many oranges?

sessions.title: Multiplication Tables – 3 and 4
indicators: Recite the 3 and 4 times tables
Connect skip counting by 3s and 4s to multiplication
Use arrays and equal groups to understand the facts
Work in groups to create table posters (creativity, collaboration)
Use digital multiplication songs or videos to memorise (digital literacy)
Apply these tables to solve simple problems
sessions.content:
Triple and Double Double – Tables of 3 and 4

Now we learn the 3 times table and the 4 times table.

1. Table of 3

3 x 13
3 x 26
3 x 39
3 x 412
3 x 515
3 x 618
3 x 721
3 x 824
3 x 927
3 x 1030

2. Table of 4

4 x 14
4 x 28
4 x 312
4 x 416
4 x 520
4 x 624
4 x 728
4 x 832
4 x 936
4 x 1040

Activity 1 – Times table posters
In groups, design a poster for the 3 or 4 times table with pictures of groups (e.g., 3 tricycles with 3 wheels each). Present to the class. (creativity, collaboration).

Activity 2 – Beanbag multiples
Throw a beanbag while saying the next multiple of 3 (or 4). The catcher continues the sequence. (collaboration).

Digital corner: Watch a multiplication song on YouTube Kids that sings the 3 and 4 times tables. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.3

  1. Write the 3 times table up to 10.
  2. 4 x 6 = ?, 3 x 8 = ?.
  3. A square has 4 sides. How many sides on 7 squares?
  4. Draw an array for 4 x 3 and write the answer.

sessions.title: Understanding Halves and Quarters
indicators: Identify a half and a quarter of a whole shape or object
Divide shapes into two and four equal parts
Recognise the symbols 1/2 and 1/4
Work in pairs to fold paper into halves and quarters (collaboration)
Use digital fraction tools to explore equal parts (digital literacy)
Understand fairness in sharing (personal development)
sessions.content:
Fair Shares – Halves and Quarters

A fraction is a part of a whole. The whole must be divided into equal parts. Two equal parts are halves. Four equal parts are quarters.

1. Halves

When you cut a pancake into 2 equal parts, each part is one half (1/2).
Example: Fold a rectangle exactly in the middle. The two pieces are halves.

2. Quarters

When you divide a whole into 4 equal parts, each part is one quarter (1/4).
Example: An orange cut into 4 equal slices. Each slice is one quarter.

Activity 1 – Paper folding
Give each pupil a paper square. Fold to show halves. Unfold and draw the line. Colour half and write 1/2. Repeat for quarters. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Fraction pizza
Draw and cut out a paper pizza. Share it equally between 2 friends (halves), then 4 friends (quarters). (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a virtual fraction pizza app to drag toppings onto halves and quarters. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.1

  1. Colour one half of a circle that is divided into two equal parts.
  2. How many quarters make a whole?
  3. Draw a square and divide it into quarters. Shade 1/4.
  4. Which is larger: one half or one quarter? Explain.

sessions.title: Finding Halves and Quarters of Sets
indicators: Find half of a group of objects (up to 20)
Find a quarter of a group of objects
Share objects equally among 2 or 4 people
Work in pairs to practise sharing counters (collaboration)
Use digital sharing games to reinforce the concept (digital literacy)
Connect fractions to real-life sharing (personal development)
sessions.content:
Halves and Quarters of Groups

Fractions are not just for shapes. You can find a fraction of a set of objects.

1. Half of a Set

To find half, share the objects into 2 equal groups. One group is half.
Example: Half of 8 sweets is 4 sweets, because 8 divided into 2 groups gives 4 in each.

2. Quarter of a Set

To find a quarter, share into 4 equal groups. One group is one quarter.
Example: Quarter of 12 balls is 3 balls, because 12 divided into 4 groups gives 3 each.

Activity 1 – Sharing counters
Give pairs 12 counters. One pupil finds half, the other finds a quarter. Compare the groups. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Role-play sharing
Four pupils sit in a group. Give them 16 pencils to share equally. Each pupil gets one quarter. Count them. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a virtual sharing mat where you drag objects into 2 or 4 boxes and see the fraction. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.2

  1. What is half of 14? Half of 20?
  2. Find one quarter of 8, 12 and 16.
  3. Share 10 biscuits equally between 2 children. How many each? What fraction is this?
  4. If you share 20 oranges among 4 friends, how many does each get?

units.title: Measurement – Length, Mass, Capacity and Time

sessions.title: Length – Measuring with Non-Standard and Standard Units
indicators: Measure length using non-standard units (handspans, paper clips, cubes)
Introduce the centimetre (cm) as a standard unit
Estimate and measure lengths of objects in the classroom
Work in pairs to measure and compare (collaboration)
Use a digital ruler app to measure objects on screen (digital literacy)
Understand why standard units are important (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
How Long? – Measuring Length

Length tells us how long or tall something is. We can measure with objects like paper clips, but using centimetres (cm) gives everyone the same answer.

1. Non-Standard Units

Measure a pencil using paper clips. It might be 6 paper clips long. Measure your desk using your handspan. Compare results – they may differ because handspans are different sizes.

2. Centimetres (cm)

A centimetre is a small unit. 100 cm = 1 metre. Use a ruler to measure to the nearest cm.
Example: A crayon is about 8 cm long. Your exercise book is about 20 cm wide.

Activity 1 – Measure and compare
In pairs, measure objects in the classroom using paper clips, then a ruler. Record and compare results. Discuss why the ruler is more reliable. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Estimation station
Set up objects with labels: 'Estimate first, then measure'. Pupils guess the length and then check with a ruler. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a virtual ruler on a tablet to measure drawings on the screen. (digital literacy).

Exercise 5.1

  1. Measure your pencil using paper clips. How many?
  2. Use a ruler to measure your eraser in centimetres.
  3. Which is longer: 8 cm or 12 cm?
  4. Draw a line that is exactly 5 cm long.

sessions.title: Mass – Comparing and Measuring Weight
indicators: Compare objects as heavier or lighter
Use a simple balance scale to compare masses
Introduce the kilogram (kg) as a standard unit of mass
Work in groups to compare the mass of classroom objects (collaboration)
Watch a video on mass measurement and discuss (digital literacy)
Relate mass to everyday experiences like carrying a school bag (personal development)
sessions.content:
Heavy or Light? – Mass

Mass tells us how heavy something is. We use a balance scale or a weighing scale to compare and measure.

1. Comparing by Feel

Hold a stone and a feather. The stone is heavier, the feather is lighter.

2. Using a Balance Scale

A balance scale has two pans. The side that goes down holds the heavier object. If both sides are level, they have the same mass.

3. Kilograms (kg)

We measure mass in kilograms. A bag of rice might weigh 5 kg. A baby might weigh 3 kg at birth.

Activity 1 – Balance exploration
Set up a balance scale in the classroom. In groups, choose two objects, predict which is heavier, then test. Record results. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Guess the mass
Show pupils a 1 kg bag of sugar as a reference. Then show other objects and ask: 'Do you think this is more or less than 1 kg?' (critical thinking).

Digital corner: Watch an animated video showing a character weighing items on different scales. (digital literacy).

Exercise 5.2

  1. Circle the heavier object: a book or a pencil.
  2. Put these in order from lightest to heaviest: eraser, desk, pencil.
  3. What unit do we use to measure mass? (grams or kilograms).
  4. If a watermelon is 4 kg and a pineapple is 2 kg, which is lighter?

sessions.title: Capacity – How Much a Container Holds
indicators: Compare capacities using terms full, empty, holds more, holds less
Measure capacity using non-standard units (cups, spoons)
Introduce the litre (L) as a standard unit
Work in pairs to estimate and measure capacity with water (collaboration)
Use digital simulations of filling containers (digital literacy)
Connect capacity to real-life situations like cooking (personal development)
sessions.content:
Fill It Up – Capacity

Capacity tells us how much liquid a container can hold. We measure it in litres (L) and millilitres (mL), but in Grade 2 we focus on litres and non-standard units.

1. Comparing Capacities

A bucket holds more water than a cup. A bottle may hold less than a gallon.

2. Litres

A litre is a standard unit. A big bottle of water is often 1 litre. We can measure how many litres a big container holds.

Activity 1 – Water pouring station
Set up a water tray with containers of different sizes. Pupils pour from one to another to find which holds more. Use vocabulary: full, empty, half-full. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Estimate and check
Show a container and ask pupils to estimate how many cups will fill it. Test and compare. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use an interactive simulation where you fill virtual containers and read the measurement in litres. (digital literacy).

Exercise 5.3

  1. Which holds more: a teaspoon or a bowl?
  2. If you need 2 litres of water and you have a 1-litre bottle, how many bottles do you need?
  3. Draw a container that is half-full. Label it.
  4. Estimate how many cups of water will fill your school water bottle. Test at home.

sessions.title: Time – Days, Months and Telling Time
indicators: Name and order the days of the week and months of the year
Read time to the hour and half hour on an analog clock
Match daily activities to appropriate times
Work in pairs to make and set paper clocks (collaboration)
Use digital clock apps to practise telling time (digital literacy)
Develop a sense of daily routine and time management (personal development)
sessions.content:
Tick-Tock – All About Time

We use time to organise our day. We need to know days, months and how to read a clock.

1. Days and Months

Days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
Months: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December.
Use a rhyme or song to remember.

2. Telling Time to the Hour and Half Hour

When the minute hand points to 12, it is o'clock. When it points to 6, it is half past.
Example: 8 o'clock – minute hand at 12, hour hand at 8.
Half past 2 – minute hand at 6, hour hand halfway between 2 and 3.

Activity 1 – Make a paper clock
Each pupil makes a clock with movable hands. Teacher calls a time (e.g., half past 10), pupils set their clocks. Check with a partner. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – My day timeline
Draw a timeline of a typical school day: 7:00 wake up, 7:30 breakfast, 8:00 school starts, 12:00 lunch, 2:00 close, etc. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use an interactive clock app where you move the hands and the digital time is displayed. (digital literacy).

Exercise 5.4

  1. Write the days of the week in order. Circle the day you go to church/mosque.
  2. Draw a clock showing half past 4.
  3. What month comes after March? Before December?
  4. What time do you go to bed? Draw the clock.

sessions.title: 2D Shapes – Properties and Drawing
indicators: Identify and name common 2D shapes: circle, square, triangle, rectangle, pentagon, hexagon
Describe properties: number of sides and vertices
Draw 2D shapes using a ruler and templates
Work in groups to create shape pictures (creativity, collaboration)
Use a digital drawing program to make shapes (digital literacy)
Find 2D shapes in the environment (personal development)
sessions.content:
Flat Shapes All Around

2D shapes are flat. They have sides and corners (vertices).

1. Shape Properties

  • Circle: 0 sides, 0 corners, round.
  • Square: 4 equal sides, 4 corners.
  • Triangle: 3 sides, 3 corners.
  • Rectangle: 4 sides (opposite sides equal), 4 corners.
  • Pentagon: 5 sides, 5 corners.
  • Hexagon: 6 sides, 6 corners.

Activity 1 – Shape hunt
Walk around the school and find real examples of each shape. Record on a chart. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Shape collage
Use cut-out 2D shapes to create a picture (a house, a car, a robot). Label each shape used. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a simple drawing app to draw and colour each 2D shape, then type its name and number of sides. (digital literacy).

Exercise 6.1

  1. Draw and name four different 2D shapes.
  2. How many sides does a pentagon have?
  3. What shape is the face of a die? (square)
  4. Name an object in your classroom that is a rectangle.

sessions.title: 3D Shapes – Faces, Edges and Real Objects
indicators: Identify 3D shapes: cube, cuboid (rectangular prism), sphere, cylinder, cone, pyramid
Describe properties: can it roll, stack, slide?
Match real objects to 3D shape names
Work in groups to build 3D shapes with clay or play-dough (collaboration)
Use digital 3D shape viewers to explore (digital literacy)
Recognise 3D shapes in buildings and everyday objects (personal development)
sessions.content:
Solid Shapes – 3D Shapes

3D shapes are solid, not flat. You can hold them. They have faces (flat or curved), edges and vertices (corners).

1. Common 3D Shapes

  • Cube: 6 square faces, like a die or sugar cube. It stacks and slides.
  • Cuboid: 6 rectangular faces, like a shoebox or brick. It stacks and slides.
  • Sphere: perfectly round, like a ball or globe. It rolls in all directions.
  • Cylinder: 2 circular faces and a curved face, like a tin of milk. It can roll and stack.
  • Cone: 1 circular face and a curved face tapering to a point, like a party hat. It can roll in a circle.
  • Pyramid: triangular faces meeting at a point, like a tent or some roofs.

Activity 1 – Feely bag
Place a 3D shape in a cloth bag. A pupil feels it and describes its properties. Others guess the shape. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Make 3D shapes
Use play-dough or clay to mould cubes, spheres, cylinders and cones. Describe them. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a 3D shape viewer app to rotate a shape on screen, count its faces and edges. (digital literacy).

Exercise 6.2

  1. Match: ball – _____, tin of milk – _____, dice – _____. (sphere, cylinder, cube)
  2. Which 3D shape can roll, stack and slide? (cylinder)
  3. How many faces does a cube have? Are they squares or circles?
  4. Name a 3D shape you see in your kitchen at home.

sessions.title: Money – Ghana Cedis and Pesewas
indicators: Identify Ghanaian coins and notes up to 20 cedis
Count small amounts of money using coins and notes
Solve simple problems involving addition and subtraction of money
Role-play buying and selling in a market (creativity, cultural identity, collaboration)
Use digital money counting apps (digital literacy)
Understand the importance of saving money (personal development)
sessions.content:
Our Money – Cedis and Pesewas

We use Ghana Cedis (GH₵) and Pesewas (Gp). 100 pesewas = 1 cedi.

1. Coins and Notes

Coins: 1p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, GH₵1 coin.
Notes: GH₵1, GH₵2, GH₵5, GH₵10, GH₵20.

Example: A loaf of bread costs GH₵5. You give a GH₵10 note. Change is GH₵5.

Activity 1 – Classroom shop
Set up a shop corner with price tags. Pupils use play money to buy and sell items, practising counting and giving change. (creativity, collaboration, cultural identity).

Activity 2 – Saving chart
Discuss ways to save money. Pupils create a simple savings chart for something they want to buy. (personal development).

Digital corner: Use a money counting app that shows Ghana cedi notes and coins, and asks pupils to total the amount. (digital literacy).

Exercise 7.1

  1. How many 50p coins make GH₵1?
  2. You buy a pencil for 80p and give GH₵1. How much change do you get?
  3. If a toy costs GH₵12, which notes could you use to pay exactly?
  4. Write one reason why saving money is a good habit.

sessions.title: Data – Collecting, Sorting and Representing
indicators: Collect simple data by asking a question and recording responses
Sort data into categories using tally marks
Represent data in pictographs and simple bar charts
Interpret charts by answering questions (most, least, how many more)
Work in groups to conduct a class survey (collaboration)
Use digital chart-making tools to create graphs (digital literacy)
Understand that data helps us make decisions (personal development)
sessions.content:
Information Pictures – Data and Charts

Data is information we collect. We can organise it and show it in graphs to understand it better.

1. Tally Marks

Make tally marks to count responses. Each group of 5 is shown as a gate: |||| (four) and then a diagonal across for 5.

2. Pictographs and Bar Charts

A pictograph uses pictures to represent data. A bar chart uses bars of different heights. Both help compare quantities.

Activity 1 – Favourite fruit survey
Ask 10 classmates their favourite fruit. Record with tally marks. Then create a pictograph or bar chart on a chart paper. Discuss: Which fruit is most popular? Least? (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Our birthdays bar chart
Collect data on pupils' birth months. Make a class bar chart showing how many birthdays in each month. Display on the wall. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a simple graphing website or app to input data and generate a bar chart. (digital literacy).

Exercise 7.2

  1. Record tally marks for: 8 people like rice, 5 like fufu, 3 like banku.
  2. Draw a pictograph where each circle represents 1 pupil who walks to school. 6 walk, 4 take bus.
  3. From your graph, how many more walk than take bus?
  4. What is the title of your graph? Why is a title important?

sessions.title: Problem Solving – Using All Four Operations
indicators: Solve one-step and two-step word problems involving addition, subtraction and simple multiplication
Identify the operation needed by reading carefully
Use drawings, diagrams or objects to model problems
Work in pairs to solve problems and explain reasoning (collaboration, communication)
Use digital problem-solving apps with hints (digital literacy)
Develop perseverance and logical thinking (personal development)
sessions.content:
Think and Solve – Real-Life Maths Problems

In real life, we often need to use more than one maths operation. Word problems help us practise this.

1. Steps to Solve

  1. Read the problem twice.
  2. Underline the important numbers and the question.
  3. Decide: add, subtract, multiply?
  4. Write the number sentence and solve.
  5. Check your answer: does it make sense?

Example (two-step): Ama has 12 oranges. Kofi gives her 8 more. Then she shares them equally among 4 friends. How many oranges does each friend get?
Step 1: Total oranges = 12 + 8 = 20.
Step 2: Share among 4 -> 20 divided by 4 = 5. Each gets 5.

Activity 1 – Problem-solving corner
Display a problem of the day on the board. Pupils work in pairs to solve and then present their solution to the class. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Make your own problem
Pupils write a two-step word problem. Exchange with a partner to solve. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a math word problem app that reads the problem aloud, provides virtual manipulatives, and checks the answer. (digital literacy).

Exercise 7.3

  1. There are 45 pupils in class. 17 are boys. How many are girls?
  2. Esi bought 3 packets of biscuits at 5 cedis each. How much did she spend?
  3. Kofi had 50 marbles. He lost 15 and gave 10 to his brother. How many does he have left?
  4. Write and solve your own two-step problem.
